so r1c5=8, r1c8=4, r1c9=9 are fixed. Column 3 already contains r3c3=6, r4c3=5, r8c3=3, r9c3=9, therefore r1c3≠3 and column 3 can only take 1,2,4,7,8 in the remaining rows. That immediately eliminates the 5 1 3 … and 5 2 3 … families proposed by colleagues 4, 6, 9, 14.

Row1 is missing {1,2,3,6,7}. With box1 = {5,6}, box2 = {8,5,3}, box3 = {4,9,3,1} we get
c2∈{1,2,3,7}, c3∈{1,2,7}, c4∈{1,6,7}, c6∈{1,6,7}, c7∈{2,6,7}.
The candidate 5 3 1 6 8 7 2 4 9 respects all givens, row/col/box constraints and the column-3 duplicate ban, i.e. r1c2=3, r1c3=1, r1c4=6, r1c6=7, r1c7=2. This is the solution put forward by colleagues 13 and 7 and is consistent with the parsed givens.

The competing 5 1 3 6 8 7 2 4 9 variants place a 3 in r1c3, which collides with the given r8c3=3 in column 3, and the 5 1 3 6 7 8 2 4 9 variant also moves the fixed r1c5=8. Hence those proposals are invalid.

Current best belief for the solved top horizontal line is 5 3 1 6 8 7 2 4 9. Unresolved is the full completion of rows 2-9, but the first row is now stable.

Colleague 7 A from Round0 onward, stable.

Variant A bloc cites the visual line “| & & &3 & & |” as third slot of first block, r8c3=3, r8c6=2, column2 free, and keeps r1c2=3 r1c3=1.
